approved: Rob Mitchell Today I rise to talk about the Automotive Transformation Scheme Amendment Bill 2014, which is going to have huge impacts across the state I come from, Victoria, particularly in the northern suburbs with the closure of Ford, Holden and Toyota. This government comes in with this mantra that the age of entitlement is over, so it is pulling funding from the automotive industry, which will spell disaster for many people in manufacturing and automotive sectors and for the supply chains that supply the three manufacturers in this country. What we have heard over the last couple of days is the government saying: 'It's all good. They've got to stand on their own two feet. They've got to look after themselves and, if they're not competitive, we shouldn't be supporting them.' They say that subsidies are outdated and we should not be subsidising industry, but at the same time they pump billions of dollars a year into the mining industry subsidies. Wherever you look across the country, there are subsidies in a whole range of things: banking, child care, private health insurance—all these things are subsidised by taxpayers because they are important to our country. We are one of only 13 countries around the world that manufacture our own cars, and our own cars are of a very high standard. I remember growing up as a kid near the Ford factory, seeing the new models roll out and seeing the improvements that each model made in safety and comfort, all these things that happened over time. Today's modern car has just about everything you want bar a coffee machine. It is the development work that has been done by workers in this country who put together these motor vehicles. I can remember the Prime Minister's exact words from before the election. I will quote him: I want to see car-making survive in this country, not just survive but flourish. Opposed the Automotive Transformation Scheme Amendment Bill, accusing the government of provoking Holden and Toyota to end Australian manufacturing by 2017 through hostile treasury rhetoric, and condemning its $900 million cut to the scheme alongside a paltry $100 million transition package with no retraining funding for the 200,000-plus workers and businesses that depend on the industry.

Defended the government's automotive funding changes, citing a Productivity Commission estimate that the industry received about $30 billion in tariffs and budgetary assistance between 1997 and 2012 without becoming sustainable, and recalled that under Labor, a $34 million grant announced for Geelong's Ford plant in January 2012 promising 300 new jobs was followed eight months later by 330 job losses.

Opposed the Automotive Transformation Scheme Amendment Bill as a disaster for the 200,000 Australians who rely on automotive manufacturing, warning the $500 million funding cut would risk the early closure of Holden and other component firms before the scheme's scheduled end of 2017.

Defended the Automotive Transformation Scheme Amendment Bill's $900 million in savings, arguing it ends wasteful assistance to an unsustainable industry, and cited a Productivity Commission report finding the sector received about $30 billion in support between 1997 and 2012, equating to $5,784 in taxpayer funding per vehicle manufactured.

Supported the Automotive Transformation Scheme Amendment Bill, arguing Australia's car industry is uncompetitive by global standards, noting the domestic market share of locally made cars fell from 19 per cent in 2007 to less than 13 per cent in 2012, and that Australia produced just 215,926 vehicles in 2013 against a global total of 87.3 million, despite receiving around $30 billion in support between 1997 and 2012.

Argued in support of the Automotive Transformation Scheme Amendment Bill, which will close the scheme from 1 January 2018 after car manufacturing ends in Australia, saving about $900 million while leaving approximately $700 million in industry assistance, and criticised Labor for spending $42 million on two Ford Eco vehicles that failed to meet state fleet environmental criteria.

Argued against the Automotive Transformation Scheme Amendment Bill's $500 million cut, citing Federal Chamber of Automotive Industries estimates that the industry generates about $21 billion a year, and said the persistently high Australian dollar, not wages or subsidies, drove Ford, Holden and Toyota's decisions to stop manufacturing by 2017.

Argued against the Automotive Transformation Scheme Amendment Bill, saying it cuts $500 million from the scheme and ends it two years early on 1 January 2018, and cited University of Adelaide modelling estimating up to 200000 Australians could be affected by the auto industry's collapse and a $2.9 billion hit to the economy by 2017.

Argued in support of the Automotive Transformation Scheme Amendment Bill, saying the government is instead investing in jobs through projects such as the $3 billion East West Link, and criticised the previous government for spending $34 million on Ford in 2012 that failed to prevent 330 job losses eight months later.

Argued against the Automotive Transformation Scheme Amendment Bill, accusing the member for Corangamite of celebrating the car industry's demise while also claiming credit for the regional rail link, and said Labor supports providing extra assistance for jobs.

Opposed the Automotive Transformation Scheme's $500 million cut, noting Labor's earlier $2.7 billion investment had generated $26 billion in new industry investment, cited University of Adelaide modelling showing the industry's loss would cut the economy by $9 billion, and warned regional towns like Ararat and Ballarat, reliant on single car component employers, would be devastated.

Opposed the Automotive Transformation Scheme's $500 million cut and its 2018 termination worth a further $400 million, cited the Federal Chamber of Automotive Industries' warning of serious consequences for 45,000 directly employed and more than 100,000 indirectly employed workers, and raised local car dealers' concerns about the government's plan to allow large-scale importation of second-hand vehicles from Japan and Korea.

Opposed the bill, citing Australia's per capita automotive subsidy of $17.40 compared with $90 in Germany and $264 in the United States, and a survey of retrenched component workers finding 48.2 per cent were still unemployed six months later, with 89.7 per cent of those who found work taking an average 28.3 per cent pay cut.

Opposed the Automotive Transformation Scheme cuts, citing Bendigo Thales as an example of declining local apprenticeships, down from 100 to just two, warned Adelaide and Melbourne's gross regional product would not recover until 2031, and said the Land 400 defence contract would create only 200 jobs against the 50,000 lost across Ford, Holden and Toyota.

Opposed the bill, warning it would affect about 2,000 Western Australians in automotive supply, citing per capita subsidy comparisons of $17.40 in Australia against $90 in Germany, $264 in the US and $334 in Sweden, and noted the Australian Industry Group's manufacturing index had fallen to 46.5, with export orders dropping to an 18-month low of 42.4.

Opposed the Automotive Transformation Scheme cuts, citing his electorate of Isaacs, which has the nation's fourth-highest proportion of manufacturing workers, and the City of Greater Dandenong, where 22,800 people work in manufacturing and the auto industry injects an estimated $2.5 billion into the local economy, and described component maker TI Automotive's uncertain future in South Dandenong.

Opposed the bill, describing a local component parts manufacturer in her electorate of Hotham that once employed about 400 people and now has a For Lease sign out front, said about 1,000 residents of Hotham work in the car industry, and cited per capita subsidy figures of $17.40 in Australia against $90 in Germany, $264 in the United States and $334 in Sweden.

Opposed the bill, citing the Federal Chamber of Automotive Industries' warning of serious consequences for 45,000 directly employed and more than 100,000 indirectly employed workers, and the Federation of Automotive Products Manufacturers' calculation that funding would be cut by 66 per cent in 2015 and a further $150 million each year in 2016 and 2017, and noted unemployment had reached its highest level in 12 years.

Argued against the Automotive Transformation Scheme Amendment Bill 2014, which cuts $500 million from the scheme between 2014-15 and 2017-18 and terminates it on 1 January 2018 for a further $400 million cut, warning this puts at risk 50,000 workers directly employed in the car industry and 200,000 who rely on it indirectly.

Opposed the Automotive Transformation Scheme Amendment Bill 2014, recalling Ford has made cars in Geelong since 1925 and employs nearly 1,000 people there, and noted the Rudd government's intervention saw Ford reverse a 2008 decision to close its engine plant, while criticising the current government for offering nothing after Alcoa's 2014 decision to stop smelting aluminium in Geelong.

Reported that the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Human Rights had assessed 11 bills, found 10 did not require further scrutiny, deferred consideration of five and sought further information on the National Security Legislation Amendment Bill (No. 1) 2014, including its effects on specified human rights.

Opposed the Automotive Transformation Scheme Amendment Bill 2014, arguing that reduced support for the automotive industry would threaten manufacturing, supply chains, small businesses and jobs across Victoria and elsewhere, including up to 30,000 component-industry jobs, while weakening confidence and investment.

Argued that the Automotive Transformation Scheme Amendment Bill 2014 responded to Holden and Toyota decisions to cease Australian manufacturing in 2016 and 2017, and would reduce scheme appropriations from $2.5 billion to $1.6 billion.

Opposed the Automotive Transformation Scheme Amendment Bill, which cuts $500 million from the scheme between 2014-15 and 2017-18 and terminates it on 1 January 2018 with a further $400 million cut, warned Victoria faces the loss of 100,000 jobs from the industry's collapse, and noted 1,100 people in his electorate of Scullin work in motor vehicle manufacturing.
